lines.speaker: CHAP
lines.visual: card:Chapter Seven · Pennsylvania|George Wolf · Penn's state

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Easton, Pennsylvania. 1833. A man named Charles Getter is to be hanged for murder. The crowd that comes to watch is enormous. Estimates run from fifteen to twenty thousand people.
lines.caption: Easton, Pennsylvania. 1833. A man named Charles Getter is to be hanged for murder. The crowd that comes to watch is enormous. Estimates run from fifteen to twenty thousand people.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: The execution is moved out of town to an island in the river. The first attempt fails. The second one doesn't. And the next year, the governor signs a law ending public executions in Pennsylvania.
lines.caption: The execution is moved out of town to an island in the river. The first attempt fails. The second one doesn't. And the next year, the governor signs a law ending public executions in Pennsylvania.

lines.speaker: PE
lines.say: Quakers, hear ye, from the Palestra! A grim start, friends, but a humane end.
lines.caption: Quakers, hear ye, from the Palestra! A grim start, friends, but a humane end.

lines.speaker: G
lines.say: Twenty thousand people to watch a hanging? What was wrong with these people?
lines.caption: Twenty thousand people to watch a hanging? What was wrong with these people?

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Not enough schools, Gary. Which brings us to the governor. George Wolf. Pennsylvania's seventh.
lines.caption: Not enough schools, Gary. Which brings us to the governor. George Wolf. Pennsylvania's seventh.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: George Wolf was born August 12th, 1777, in Allen Township, Northampton County, He studied at a local classical academy, read law, and was admitted to the bar in 1799.
lines.caption: George Wolf was born August 12th, 1777, in Allen Township, Northampton County, He studied at a local classical academy, read law, and was admitted to the bar in 1799.
lines.visual: card:Fact 1 of 7|Born 1777 in Northampton County · admitted to the bar in 1799

lines.speaker: PE
lines.say: No Penn for Mister Wolf. A country academy and a stack of law books. Your humble servant approves.
lines.caption: No Penn for Mister Wolf. A country academy and a stack of law books. Your humble servant approves.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: He went to the United States House in 1824, a protectionist and a Jackson man. In 1829 he beat Joseph Ritner for governor, and in 1832 he beat Ritner again.
lines.caption: He went to the United States House in 1824, a protectionist and a Jackson man. In 1829 he beat Joseph Ritner for governor, and in 1832 he beat Ritner again.
lines.visual: card:Fact 2 of 7|U.S. Congress 1824 to 1829 · elected governor in 1829 and 1832

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: He served on the board of Lafayette College in Easton from 1827 until he died. He would make schools the fight of his life.
lines.caption: He served on the board of Lafayette College in Easton from 1827 until he died. He would make schools the fight of his life.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Now the count. Before 1790 Pennsylvania didn't have a governor. It had a Supreme Executive Council, and that council had a president. Seven of them.
lines.caption: Now the count. Before 1790 Pennsylvania didn't have a governor. It had a Supreme Executive Council, and that council had a president. Seven of them.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: The sixth president was Benjamin Franklin. The seventh was Thomas Mifflin, a 1760 graduate of the College of Philadelphia, which is Penn. Mifflin then became the first governor under the 1790 constitution.
lines.caption: The sixth president was Benjamin Franklin. The seventh was Thomas Mifflin, a 1760 graduate of the College of Philadelphia, which is Penn. Mifflin then became the first governor under the 1790 constitution.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Count from 1790, and it's Mifflin, McKean, Snyder, Findlay, Hiester, Shulze, and seven, George Wolf.
lines.caption: Count from 1790, and it's Mifflin, McKean, Snyder, Findlay, Hiester, Shulze, and seven, George Wolf.
lines.visual: card:Fact 3 of 7|Counting governors from 1790, George Wolf is Pennsylvania's 7th

lines.speaker: PE
lines.say: And Franklin was the very first president of the Academy and College of Philadelphia. Penn's own. Hear ye.
lines.caption: And Franklin was the very first president of the Academy and College of Philadelphia. Penn's own. Hear ye.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Franklin is the story in miniature. He enslaved at least seven people over his life and ran ads selling enslaved people in his newspaper. In his last years he was president of the Pennsylvania Abolition Society. Both of those are Franklin.
lines.caption: Franklin is the story in miniature. He enslaved at least seven people over his life and ran ads selling enslaved people in his newspaper. In his last years he was president of the Pennsylvania Abolition Society. Both of those are Franklin.
lines.visual: card:Benjamin Franklin|Enslaver, then president of the Pennsylvania Abolition Society

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Getter was hanged for the murder of a woman named Margaret Lawall. And the crowd that came to watch, up to twenty thousand people, was bigger than most towns in the state. Pennsylvania's leaders looked at that crowd and decided hanging had become a show. Wolf ended the show.
lines.caption: Getter was hanged for the murder of a woman named Margaret Lawall. And the crowd that came to watch, up to twenty thousand people, was bigger than most towns in the state. Pennsylvania's leaders looked at that crowd and decided hanging had become a show. Wolf ended the show.

lines.speaker: PE
lines.say: A state that turns a hanging into a holiday has a schooling problem. Mister Wolf saw the connection.
lines.caption: A state that turns a hanging into a holiday has a schooling problem. Mister Wolf saw the connection.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Back to Wolf. Governors before him had tried to build a statewide system of common schools, open to every child, not just families who could pay. They failed. Wolf pushed, and in 1834 Pennsylvania passed its free school law.
lines.caption: Back to Wolf. Governors before him had tried to build a statewide system of common schools, open to every child, not just families who could pay. They failed. Wolf pushed, and in 1834 Pennsylvania passed its free school law.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: He's remembered as the father of Pennsylvania's public schools. Easton put up a memorial gateway in his honor in 1888.
lines.caption: He's remembered as the father of Pennsylvania's public schools. Easton put up a memorial gateway in his honor in 1888.
lines.visual: card:Fact 4 of 7|Remembered as the father of Pennsylvania's public-school system

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: And on April 10th, 1834, he signed the law that ended public executions. Charles Getter was the last.
lines.caption: And on April 10th, 1834, he signed the law that ended public executions. Charles Getter was the last.
lines.visual: card:Fact 5 of 7|On April 10, 1834, he signed the law ending public executions

lines.speaker: G
lines.say: Okay. Schools and no more public hangings. That's a good year.
lines.caption: Okay. Schools and no more public hangings. That's a good year.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: It was a good spring, Gary. Then came August.
lines.caption: It was a good spring, Gary. Then came August.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: August 12th, 1834. Philadelphia. A mob of several hundred white men, many of them Irish immigrants, attacks a carousel on South Street called the Flying Horses, a place where Black and white residents mixed. Then it moves into Moyamensing and goes after Black-owned homes and buildings.
lines.caption: August 12th, 1834. Philadelphia. A mob of several hundred white men, many of them Irish immigrants, attacks a carousel on South Street called the Flying Horses, a place where Black and white residents mixed. Then it moves into Moyamensing and goes after Black-owned homes and buildings.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: The mob grew to four or five hundred. Mayor John Swift gathered a posse of about three hundred. On the first night, eighteen men were arrested. By the end, about sixty. The committee that studied the damage put it at around four to six thousand dollars. Lucretia Mott, the Quaker abolitionist, wrote about it in her letters.
lines.caption: The mob grew to four or five hundred. Mayor John Swift gathered a posse of about three hundred. On the first night, eighteen men were arrested. By the end, about sixty. The committee that studied the damage put it at around four to six thousand dollars. Lucretia Mott, the Quaker abolitionist, wrote about it in her letters.
lines.visual: card:Philadelphia, August 12 to 14, 1834|A mob of 400 to 500 · about 60 arrests

lines.speaker: G
lines.say: Sixty arrests for forty-four buildings and two people dead.
lines.caption: Sixty arrests for forty-four buildings and two people dead.

lines.speaker: PE
lines.say: Philadelphia counted the windows, Gary. It was slower to count the people.
lines.caption: Philadelphia counted the windows, Gary. It was slower to count the people.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: For three nights the mob attacks Black homes and churches. The African Presbyterian Church is targeted. The Wharton Street Church is destroyed. When it's over, forty-four buildings are gone and two people are dead.
lines.caption: For three nights the mob attacks Black homes and churches. The African Presbyterian Church is targeted. The Wharton Street Church is destroyed. When it's over, forty-four buildings are gone and two people are dead.
lines.visual: card:Fact 6 of 7|The 1834 Philadelphia race riot, while Wolf was governor · 44 buildings destroyed, 2 dead

lines.speaker: PE
lines.say: In the City of Brotherly Love, friends. The name was a promise, not a description.
lines.caption: In the City of Brotherly Love, friends. The name was a promise, not a description.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: The school law was a promise to every child in Pennsylvania. That August, the city showed who it actually protected.
lines.caption: The school law was a promise to every child in Pennsylvania. That August, the city showed who it actually protected.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: And it got worse. Wolf lost in 1835 to Ritner when his own Democrats split. And in 1838 Pennsylvania wrote a new constitution that took the vote away from Black men. Robert Purvis led the protest, the Appeal of Forty Thousand Citizens Threatened with Disfranchisement. Black Pennsylvanians didn't get the vote back until 1870.
lines.caption: And it got worse. Wolf lost in 1835 to Ritner when his own Democrats split. And in 1838 Pennsylvania wrote a new constitution that took the vote away from Black men. Robert Purvis led the protest, the Appeal of Forty Thousand Citizens Threatened with Disfranchisement. Black Pennsylvanians didn't get the vote back until 1870.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Wolf married Mary Erb in 1798. They had eight sons and a daughter. As governor he pushed the legislature to build canals, and to raise taxes to pay the state's debts for them. Taxes are never popular.
lines.caption: Wolf married Mary Erb in 1798. They had eight sons and a daughter. As governor he pushed the legislature to build canals, and to raise taxes to pay the state's debts for them. Taxes are never popular.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Ritner won that 1835 race as an Anti-Mason, and the Democrats split between Wolf and Henry Muhlenberg. The man who built the schools lost his job to a divided party and a split vote.
lines.caption: Ritner won that 1835 race as an Anti-Mason, and the Democrats split between Wolf and Henry Muhlenberg. The man who built the schools lost his job to a divided party and a split vote.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Andrew Jackson made Wolf First Comptroller of the Treasury, and later he ran the customs house in Philadelphia. He died there on March 11th, 1840.
lines.caption: Andrew Jackson made Wolf First Comptroller of the Treasury, and later he ran the customs house in Philadelphia. He died there on March 11th, 1840.
lines.visual: card:Fact 7 of 7|Wolf Street in Philadelphia and Wolf Hall at Penn State are named for him

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: There's a Wolf Street in South Philadelphia, schools in his name in Bath and Bethlehem, and a Wolf Hall at Penn State. Not Penn. Penn State.
lines.caption: There's a Wolf Street in South Philadelphia, schools in his name in Bath and Bethlehem, and a Wolf Hall at Penn State. Not Penn. Penn State.

lines.speaker: PE
lines.say: A distinction we at Penn insist upon. Quill out.
lines.caption: A distinction we at Penn insist upon. Quill out.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: He opened the schoolhouse door. The rest of the state was still deciding who got through it.
lines.caption: He opened the schoolhouse door. The rest of the state was still deciding who got through it.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Seven states. Seven governors. Griswold, Fenner, Yates, Sullivan, Plumer, Dickerson, Wolf. Not one of them is famous. Every one of them made choices about who counted.
lines.caption: Seven states. Seven governors. Griswold, Fenner, Yates, Sullivan, Plumer, Dickerson, Wolf. Not one of them is famous. Every one of them made choices about who counted.
lines.visual: card:Lucky Seven|Griswold · Fenner · Yates · Sullivan · Plumer · Dickerson · Wolf

lines.speaker: G
lines.say: Matthew, I came in knowing one governor from back east. Now I know seven, and I'm mad at about four of them.
lines.caption: Matthew, I came in knowing one governor from back east. Now I know seven, and I'm mad at about four of them.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: That's the right number to be mad at, Gary. The Ivy League trained the men who ran these states. The question is never just who led. It's who got a say, who got left out, and who paid for it.
lines.caption: That's the right number to be mad at, Gary. The Ivy League trained the men who ran these states. The question is never just who led. It's who got a say, who got left out, and who paid for it.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Lucky seven. Keep it mid. Keep it real.
lines.caption: Lucky seven. Keep it mid. Keep it real.
